lines: Last time, we ended on a rule: a JSON entry in the log is only a commit once it's written atomically as the next version number.
Today we build exactly that, for real — reusing the same conditional-write primitive we already built, now doing the one job Delta actually asks of it.
Picture two writers racing to commit the same next version. Writer A's write lands first.
What happens to writer B? Does it overwrite A's result, merge with it somehow, or get turned away entirely?
answer: It gets rejected outright. A commit here is a single atomic write of one specific file name — there's no way for two different writers to both occupy it.
So the race has exactly one winner, decided by whichever write physically lands first, not by anything either writer can control after the fact.

lines: Here's the real write: a conditional PUT with If-None-Match, targeting the exact file the next version has to live at.
Writer A's write succeeds. Writer B sends the identical request a moment later and gets back a real precondition-failed error, not a timeout, not a merge.
So writer B lost the race. What does it actually have to check before trying again?
Because its operation was an append, the answer is nothing — an append never conflicts with anything that came before it, so it just re-aims at the new tip and wins the very next version instead.
Now change the operation. A concurrent insert lands first, at version three. A delete that started before that insert, and never saw it, tries to commit right after.
Under Delta's default isolation level, does that delete get to commit, or does it get turned back as a conflict?
answer: It commits. Delta's default level only requires that writes line up in some valid order — it doesn't require the delete to have seen everything that happened before it.
So the system is free to treat the insert as if it logically happened after the delete, even though the log says otherwise.

lines: That default is called WriteSerializable, and this is exactly its behavior: the delete commits, because the two operations can still be arranged into some valid order.
The stronger level, Serializable, would not allow this — it insists the physical order and the logical order always agree.
Push it further: make the delete's one target row the exact same row the insert just added.

WriteSerializable still lets the delete through, by that same ordering trick — but Serializable now refuses it, because letting it through would mean a reader could see a table state the log itself never actually produced.
So why did any of this ever need a separate coordinating service in the first place?

Because for years, plain object storage had no conditional write at all — two writers could both successfully publish the same version number, and nothing on the storage side would ever notice or stop it. That's the exact gap Delta's DynamoDB-based coordinator was built to close.
Once a real conditional write existed, Delta didn't stop there — it moved the whole question of truth into the catalog itself.

Twenty twenty-five's preview makes the catalog the arbiter of whether a commit succeeded. One release then hands it the commit itself, and the next hands it everything else a table can do — not a bigger lock, but one place that finally answers for the whole table.
So: a commit is one atomic, winner-take-all write of the next version. An isolation level decides which non-overlapping stories about that write are even allowed to stand.
And a catalog-managed table is what happens when a storage system stops trusting any single file to settle that question by itself.
